The tokenizer itself: minimal, single-purpose, no dead code, no over-engineering (does not attempt to handle unrelated regex features like quantifiers/alternation-counting since capture-name enumeration does not need them); doc comment accurately describes the prior bug and the fix. I independently re-implemented the tokenizer in a scratch script and cross-checked it against real new RegExp(pattern,u) semantics on 10 adversarial patterns beyond the committed RED tests: empty class [] immediately closing (JS-correct, not POSIX-literal-close-bracket), nested-looking open-bracket inside a class (literal, ignored), an escaped closing bracket inside a class correctly does not prematurely close, a real capture immediately following a class, a lookbehind (?<=...) correctly excluded (its = is not a name-start char) while a real named capture beside it is still found, a negative lookbehind (?<!...) correctly excluded, escaped literal brackets around a real capture, an escaped backslash followed by a real capture, a unicode-property escape not confusing the scanner, and duplicate named-group names across alternation (rejected upstream by new RegExp itself in Node 22, so the tokenizer never sees it, fail-closed via the null-return path, unchanged from before). Also verified that switching the scan target from compiled.source (old) to the raw input pattern string (new) cannot change capture detection: RegExp.prototype.source only re-escapes forward-slash and raw line-terminator characters relative to the input pattern, and never touches the parenthesis/question-mark/angle-bracket/name characters, so the two are structurally equivalent for this specific scan. No regressions found; no findings raised.
